subject: Tesla cut its AI spending plan by $5 billion
bodyMarkdown:
If you hold an S&P 500 fund in a TFSA, AI capital spending is most of what moved your balance this year. Last night two of the biggest spenders reported within hours of each other and went in opposite directions, which has not happened before.

## Tesla cut its own AI budget

On Wednesday's call, CFO Vaibhav Taneja said Tesla is lowering its 2026 **capital expenditure** target, the money that goes into factories and equipment rather than wages, to $20 billion from the more than $25 billion it had projected in its second quarter filing. Third quarter spending came in at $4.73 billion. Analysts had it closer to $7.95 billion on average. Tesla has now spent $13.01 billion over nine months, so even the reduced target leaves about $7 billion for the fourth quarter, against roughly $12 billion under the old guide. Musk told investors the spending gets "more meaningful" in 2027 and reaches "the tens of billions" in 2028, according to call transcripts. The build is not cancelled. It slipped a year, and he said so out loud.

## Meta went the other way the same night

Meta reported Wednesday as well. Revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, Fortune reported, while legal settlements and AI spending squeezed profit and free cash flow. CNBC's live coverage put Meta's third quarter capital spending at $34.91 billion, the most it has ever spent on equipment in a single quarter, and said Meta lifted the floor of its full year data centre range to $135 billion from $130 billion, keeping the top at $145 billion. Set those two quarters side by side. Meta spent more on equipment in ninety days than Tesla now plans to spend in all of 2026. Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon report next week, and Yahoo Finance tallied the four big hyperscalers at roughly $725 billion of 2026 capital spending, up from $410 billion last year. Tesla is the outlier here, not the trend.

## Spending less got punished

This is the part I keep turning over. Tesla generated $1.53 billion of free cash flow in a quarter analysts had modelled as a $4.92 billion burn, on Reuters figures. Investing.com reported the stock closed up 3.41% at $386.47, then fell 2.22% after hours once the lower spending guide landed late in the call. Less spending, more cash, lower price. That only adds up if investors now treat capex as the scoreboard for who wins AI, and read a $3 billion shortfall in a single quarter as a delay or as a company guarding its balance sheet. Tesla's income statement gives them something to chew on. Electrek reported operating income fell 56% to $718 million, a 2.6% operating margin against 5.8% a year earlier, with operating costs up 39% and research up 69% on AI and Optimus work.

## The takeaway

I do not read Tesla's cut as the AI boom cracking, I read it as the first big name saying the build can wait a year and getting marked down for saying so. Watch Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon next week. If all three hold or raise their capital spending guides, Tesla looks like a company with its own problems, and if any one of them trims, that $725 billion figure starts to look like a ceiling rather than a floor. For anyone holding index funds, the question worth tracking is whether the spending still arrives with revenue attached.
